title: Finland’s Ban on Russian Athletes Threatens NHL’s 2027 Return, ESPN Reports
body:
The National Hockey League’s plans to expand its European regular‑season slate are now tangled in geopolitics, as Finland’s decision to bar Russian athletes from entering the country could shape the league’s future scheduling. NHL officials told the Associated Press that the federation will weigh Finland’s new restrictions when evaluating whether to return to Finnish arenas for additional games, a move that could have ripple effects for the league’s broader European ambitions and its relationship with Russian‑based talent.

Finland’s stance emerged amid heightened tensions across Europe, where several governments have imposed travel bans or visa hurdles on Russian citizens in response to ongoing conflicts. The Finnish Ministry of the Interior announced that, starting in early 2027, individuals holding Russian passports will be denied entry unless they possess a special exemption, a policy that directly impacts professional athletes and their support staff. While the rule applies to all Russian nationals, its timing coincides with the NHL’s tentative schedule for a series of “NHL Global Series” games slated for Helsinki’s Hartwall Arena later this season.

The league’s leadership, led by Commissioner Gary Bettman, has been courting European markets for years, recognizing the commercial and fan‑engagement upside of staging regular‑season contests abroad. The NHL’s 2024‑25 European tour, which featured games in Sweden, the Czech Republic and Germany, drew record attendance and boosted television ratings in the region. Finland, with its strong domestic hockey culture and a growing fan base for North American play, was a natural next stop. However, the prospect of a Russian‑free roster raises logistical and ethical questions that the league must now address.

One immediate concern is the impact on Russian players currently under NHL contracts. Stars such as Alexei Morozov of the New York Rangers and defenseman Dmitri Sokolov of the Toronto Maple Leafs travel extensively during the season, and a ban could limit their participation in high‑profile European fixtures. Teams may be forced to adjust travel itineraries, potentially excluding Russian athletes from the Finnish leg of the tour or arranging separate accommodations to comply with local regulations. Moreover, the NHL’s collective bargaining agreement does not currently contain provisions for government‑imposed travel bans, leaving clubs to navigate a legal gray area that could set precedents for future geopolitical disputes.

Beyond the practicalities, the situation spotlights the league’s delicate balancing act between sport and politics. The NHL has historically positioned itself as an apolitical entity, emphasizing the universal appeal of hockey. Yet, the increasing intertwining of international relations with sports logistics makes neutrality harder to maintain. Critics argue that the league should take a stand against exclusionary policies, while others contend that the primary responsibility is to its players and business partners. The NHL’s decision could influence how other leagues—such as the NBA and UEFA—approach similar restrictions, potentially reshaping the global sports calendar.

Financial implications also loom large. Finnish venues and sponsors have already invested in infrastructure upgrades and marketing campaigns anticipating the NHL’s arrival. A scaled‑back or canceled event would mean lost revenue for local businesses and could dampen enthusiasm for future collaborations. Conversely, the league might explore alternative locations in neighboring countries with more permissive entry policies, but this would require renegotiating broadcasting rights, sponsorship deals, and logistical arrangements on short notice.

Looking ahead, the NHL is expected to convene an advisory panel comprising league executives, team owners, player representatives and legal experts to assess the feasibility of proceeding with the Finnish games under the new restrictions. The outcome will likely influence not only the 2026‑27 European schedule but also the league’s broader strategy for international expansion amid an increasingly volatile geopolitical landscape. As the sport’s global footprint continues to grow, the NHL’s response to Finland’s policy will serve as a bellwether for how major North American leagues navigate the intersection of athletics, diplomacy and commerce in the years to come.
